introduction-it-works-on-my-machine-is-n.core: Working code isn't production-ready. A service also needs monitoring, alerting, runbooks, capacity, dependencies understood, failure handling and an owner. Operational readiness gates check this before launch.

first_principles.problem: A new service launches, falls over under real load, and nobody knows how to debug it at 3 AM.
truths: Launch is when problems are cheapest to fix.

analogy.title: A test-kitchen dish vs. dinner service
analogy.story: Perfect in the test kitchen, but can the line produce 200 plates an hour consistently?
analogy.breaks: Readiness gates can become bureaucracy, so keep them practical and automated.

example.title: A launch that skipped readiness

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Readiness work is cheaper before launch.

example.outcome: launches that are operable from day one.

check.q: Name three things a service needs beyond working code to be production-ready.
check.a: For example, monitoring and alerting, runbooks and an owner, and validated capacity.

production-readiness-reviews-prr.core: A PRR is a structured checklist review before a service goes to production (or before SRE takes it on): SLOs, monitoring, alerting, runbooks, on-call, capacity, dependencies, failure modes, security, deploy and rollback, and DR.

first_principles.problem: Services are 'thrown over the wall' to operations with no observability or documentation.

analogy.title: A pre-flight inspection
analogy.story: Before any commercial flight, every critical system is checked against a list, however experienced the crew.
analogy.breaks: A PRR is a conversation, not just checkboxes. Use judgement on the risks.

example.title: PRR findings
flow: No timeout on payment API calls → fix

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: A smooth launch with known risks.

example.outcome: every production service meets a baseline.

points: Cover reliability, ops, resilience and change.

check.q: What's the purpose of a Production Readiness Review?
check.a: To verify a service meets operational standards (monitoring, runbooks, resilience, capacity) before going to production.

capacity-planning-science-not-guesswork.core: Capacity planning forecasts demand (peak RPS, growth, events), measures per-instance capacity through load testing, and provisions with headroom, replacing 'start with 5 big instances and see'.

first_principles.problem: Intuitive sizing either wastes money or collapses on launch day.
truths: Demand can be estimated from data and business plans.
Per-instance capacity must be measured, not assumed.
derivation: **Load test** to find per-instance capacity at your SLO latency.

analogy.title: Planning seats for a concert
analogy.story: Estimate attendance, know how many people each section holds safely, and add spare space for emergencies.
analogy.breaks: Forecasts are uncertain, so combine planning with autoscaling.

example.title: Sizing a launch
flow: Load test: 250 RPS/instance at p99 < 200 ms

check.q: Why measure per-instance capacity at your SLO latency, not at maximum throughput?
check.a: Near maximum throughput latency explodes, so the usable capacity is what meets the SLO.

the-erlang-c-formula-the-math-of-queues.core: Simple division (400 RPS / 100 per server = 4 servers) ignores randomness: requests arrive in bursts and queues form. Erlang C computes the probability of waiting and the average wait for given servers, arrival rate and service time.

first_principles.problem: Running 4 servers at 100% theoretical utilisation causes unbounded queues and latency spikes.
truths: Queueing delay grows non-linearly with utilisation.
derivation: Inputs: **arrival rate λ**, **service rate μ**, **servers c**.
Choose **c** so P(wait) or the average wait meets targets.

analogy.title: A call centre staffing model
analogy.story: Erlang C was invented to decide how many operators are needed so callers rarely wait.
analogy.breaks: It assumes Poisson arrivals and exponential service times, which real systems only approximate.

example.title: The impact of one extra server
flow: c=4 (95% util): P(wait) very high, long queues
example.outcome: capacity sized with queueing reality in mind.

check.q: Why does running servers near 100% utilisation cause latency spikes?
check.a: Random arrival bursts form queues, and waiting time grows non-linearly as utilisation approaches 100%.

the-n1-and-n07-rules-practical-capacity-.core: Two practical rules. N+1 means provision enough to survive losing one unit (instance, AZ) at peak. N/0.7 means size so peak utilisation stays around 70%, leaving room for bursts and queueing.

first_principles.problem: Engineers need quick, safe sizing rules beyond theoretical queueing models.
truths: Around 70% utilisation balances cost and latency.

analogy.title: Seats in a car pool
analogy.story: Plan for 70% full, so latecomers fit, and keep a spare car in case one breaks down.
analogy.breaks: The 0.7 factor is a heuristic. Latency-sensitive services may need lower utilisation.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: It survives an AZ loss at peak without saturation.

check.q: What does the N+1 rule protect against?
check.a: Losing one unit of capacity (an instance or AZ) at peak without degrading service.
